rail_guard.text: Queen Street Station. Trains for every station you have visited in Great Britain. Mind the gap, the step, and the pigeon.
Hop aboard! Where to? Air adhart, as they say: onwards.

then.text: Raining again? That's why the Subway's underground. Glasgow's smartest idea, and it's from 1896.
Sunshine! Folk are walking instead of taking the Subway. It'll feel quite lonely down there the day.
Rush hour on the Clockwork Orange. Round and round, everyone heading home. Mind the doors, pal.

glw_subway.text: {greeting} The Glasgow Subway is just one circle, opened in 1896, and it's the third oldest underground in the world after London and Budapest. We call it the Clockwork Orange. Politely, it's orange.
It goes round and round, so you can't get on the wrong train. You can only get on the right train in the wrong direction.

then.text: Raining? Perfect day for Kelvingrove. It's dry, it's free, and Sir Roger the elephant never complains.
Sunshine in Glasgow! Folk'll be out in Kelvingrove Park, so you'll have Sir Roger all to yourself.

glw_guide.text: Welcome to Kelvingrove! Mind the elephant, he's called Sir Roger, and he's under glass. Be impressed, quietly.
There's a Spitfire in the ceiling, a Dalí of Christ on a cross seen from above, and a great pipe organ that plays most days. The gallery's free, so don't get any ideas about paying.

then.text: Rain? We built ships in worse than this. Forty years on the Clyde and I've never been properly dry.
Fog on the Clyde takes me back. You'd hear the yards before you saw them. Clang, clang, clang, all day.
I like the Clyde at dusk. The cranes go all dark against the sky, like great big iron giraffes.

glw_riveter.text: {greeting} I worked on the Clyde for forty years. Whole ships grew from the river like a magic trick, and it took ten thousand of us to do the trick.
That crane there lifted locomotives. Glasgow built engines for half the planet. The other half wanted them too.

then.text: Rain's nae bother, I've got a brolly and a waterproof song. It's mostly about rain, so it fits.
Nae point playing in this wind, the tune goes halfway to Paisley before anyone hears it.
Late set in George Square. The streetlights are on and the pigeons have gone to bed, so it's just us.

glw_busker.text: Nae bother in George Square. It's a cracking spot for a tune. The statues are a captive audience, and the pigeons are fair critics.
A wee bit of Gaelic? Ciamar a tha thu, 'how are you'. Say it and people will smile. Say it badly and they'll smile more.

then.text: A paisley scarf. Pattern on pattern. Mackintosh would have wept, then redesigned it.
Mackintosh would've designed a better umbrella. Tall, straight lines, a wee rose on the handle.
Up early for life drawing. Nobody's awake enough to talk, which is ideal. I can just draw.

glw_artstudent.text: The Glasgow School of Art made this city a design capital. Charles Rennie Mackintosh's work is all over town: tall chairs, roses and a lot of straight lines.
Mackintosh liked everything to match. He designed the building, the chairs, the cutlery and, probably, the weather.

then.text: You danced it. You won it. Well, you danced it. The cup's still in my cupboard, with a sign on it that says NOT YET.
Fiona and Ruaridh, beaten at their own game! That's never happened, not in the hall's whole history. Well, once, in 2011, but nobody speaks of it.
Here, a bit of tablet for the road. Mind your fillings. Mine are in a drawer in Paisley.

else.text: Strip the Willow starts at seven, and the callers, Fiona and Ruaridh, are a double act. Two on two. They're lovely, and they're not fair.
Walk past them and they'll ask you to dance. There's no polite way to say no. I've tried.

glasgow_fox_watcher.text: Shh. There's a vixen in the park, just past the bins. Red torch only, foxes don't mind red light.
Glasgow's got more foxes than you'd think. They come out when the city goes quiet, and they own the place.
One fox here nicks chips from the bins every Friday. Very regular. You could set the Subway by him.

glasgow_night_nurse.text: Off to the night shift at the Royal Infirmary. Twelve hours, a flask of tea and a packet of teacakes.
Night shifts are quiet, until they're not. Still, I wouldn't swap the folk I work with for anything.
Glasgow at night's got a wee glow to it. Even the rain looks friendly under the streetlights.

isles_gina.text: {greeting} Buongiorno! I'm Gina. My great-granny came from Barga, in Tuscany. So many Barghigiani came to Scotland that they call Barga the most Scottish town in Italy.
The Italians gave Scotland its cafes, its ice cream and a fair few of its chip shops. Scotland gave us the rain. Fair swap.
In 1940 my great-grandad was lifted as an enemy alien, after forty years in Glasgow. He should have been on the Arandora Star. He missed it, by luck. Plenty didn't.
